intent: 17 new dishes to go with the 13 batch-1 candidates being re-attempted, making 30. Batch 1 converted 11 of 24, and it leaned heavily on drinks, sides and sweets; this one is weighted toward things a household actually eats for lunch and dinner, and toward Egyptian, because the catalogue is 25.0% Egyptian against a ≥30% goal. Nine of the seventeen are Egyptian and none is an invented Egyptian variant of a foreign dish. Protein spread is deliberate: liver, sausage, whole chicken, eggs, white cheese and chicken breast rather than another round of the same three. Every list is five lines or fewer counting water, salt and oil.

candidates.name: Macaroni in Red Sauce
candidates.note: Probably the most-cooked weeknight dinner in Egypt and the catalogue does not have it. Distinct from pasta-pomodoro: this is tomato PASTE fried with garlic, not fresh tomatoes and basil.

candidates.name: Rice with Vermicelli
candidates.note: The base under half the Egyptian dinners in the catalogue, and it has never been a recipe of its own. The vermicelli row is used by almost nothing.

candidates.name: Alexandrian Liver
candidates.note: The Alexandria sandwich. Nothing in the catalogue uses the liver row, and offal is a protein group with no representation at all.

candidates.name: Egyptian Sausage in Tomato
candidates.note: Four lines, a pan, and a protein the catalogue otherwise never cooks.

candidates.name: Whole Chicken in the Oven with Cumin
candidates.note: Friday lunch. The whole-chicken row was added in Stage 2A specifically because a whole bird is not chicken breast, and no recipe has ever used it.

candidates.name: Eggs Scrambled with Tomato
candidates.note: Four lines and it is dinner when there is nothing in the house. Distinct from shakshuka, which keeps the yolks whole and adds peppers and cheese.

candidates.name: White Cheese with Tomato and Mint
candidates.note: The plate that sits on an Egyptian breakfast table beside the foul. Breakfast is still the thinnest meal type in the catalogue.

candidates.name: Fried Aubergine with Garlic and Vinegar
candidates.note: A mezze plate in every Egyptian home, and cheap. The vinegar-and-garlic dressing is what makes it Egyptian rather than generic fried aubergine.

candidates.name: Cheese Sambousek
candidates.note: Ramadan table, four lines. Uses bought phyllo, which is what an Egyptian kitchen actually does.

candidates.name: Spanish Potato Omelette
candidates.note: Five lines, feeds four, keeps cold. One of the best cheap mains there is and the Commons category is enormous.

candidates.name: Lemon and Oregano Chicken Skewers
candidates.note: Five lines, and close enough to shish tawook that an Egyptian cook already owns everything in it.

candidates.name: Greek Spinach Rice
candidates.note: A one-pot vegan main at five lines. The catalogue's vegan mains are mostly legumes.

candidates.name: Yogurt Flatbread
candidates.note: Five pantry lines and a hot pan. No oven needed, which matters in a kitchen that may not have one.

candidates.name: Crumbed Chicken Cutlet
candidates.note: This is بانيه — one of the most ordered things in Egypt — and the catalogue has no crumbed cutlet at all. Tagged asian because the dish is katsu; the Egyptian name is in the title.

candidates.name: Cabbage and Carrot Slaw
candidates.note: Sold beside every roast chicken in Egypt. Five lines, no cooking, keeps for days.

candidates.name: Potato and Egg Salad
candidates.note: Cheap, filling, and the Commons category is very large.

candidates.name: Pocket Flatbread
candidates.note: Five lines, nothing perishable, and it is the bread half the levantine recipes in the catalogue assume you have.
